title: Baseline before any archive file
blurb: No records yet. The line starts from one statement: Kevin Jr., born in Montréal in 1985, and his father Kevin John Duska, born in 1962. Everything above the father is either something Kevin said before this rebuild began (logged as priors, not as findings) or an inference. A first pass through public catalogues turned up where the parish registers for Senné and Iňačovce are held and one conflict to settle early: the 1869 census is reported not to survive for Ung county in the usual collection. Eight hypotheses are on the board, each with a confidence and a named test, so later batches can score them.

title: Senne Interesting Pages: a bishop's circulars, 1837 to 1840
blurb: Ten consecutive openings from one manuscript volume. It is not a register. It is a parish copy-book of circulars sent by János Hám, Bishop of Szatmár, and his vicar general between June 1837 and January 1840, checked and countersigned by the district vice-archdeacon. Internal evidence places it in the Nagykapos district of Ung county: a district meeting at N. Kapos on 14 May 1839, repeated business about the district library at Ungvár, and a local note recording a silk veil given by Theresia Kulin in August 1838. No Duska is named on any page. For the tree this batch is context. It shows the archive owner was working through Roman Catholic parish material filed under Senné, which nudges H-004 and H-005 up a little. It also gives a tariff of church fees from 1838 and a ten-year-old missing-husband notice that is kept under Curiosities.

title: Čičarovce: the first Demko on paper
blurb: One file: a single line cut from a baptism register. Entry 36 is Mihály, a legitimate son, born 19 August 1882 and baptised the next day. Father Demkó György, Greek Catholic, farmer. Mother Hreskó Mária, Roman Catholic. Home Viszoka, house 132. Godparents Varga Mihály and Hreskó Anna, both Roman Catholic. The strip has no page header, so the parish (Čičarovce) rests on the owner's file name. This is the first record that could connect to Ahn 9, Maria Demko, and it does not name her. What it does is put a Greek Catholic Demko farmer in Ung county in 1882, married across the rite line to a Roman Catholic. Two rival placements go on the board: Mihály as Maria's father (H-012) or as her brother (H-013). A third hypothesis (H-014) offers a reason her own record would be in Uzhhorod: if she was born after October 1895, the county copy of the civil register went to Ungvár. Nothing is added to the direct line yet. The three people are held as unplaced candidates.

title: Coordinator ledger v1 and first note from the Demko agent
blurb: No new files. Two documents from the other chats arrived through the Project. The coordinator relays that Kevin named Ahn 4 as Stefan Duska and Ahn 8 as Mihaly Duska in the Demko chat, so both go on the line as stated, and H-003 (a Ján or John at Ahn 4 or 8) is refuted by statement. The Demko agent's copy of the 1882 strip has the same checksum as mine and the two readings agree on every field. Its reading of the officiant, Csurgovich, holds up on a second look and changes the picture: with a Greek Catholic father, a Greek Catholic clerical surname, and the 1868 rule that sons follow the father's church, the book is more likely Greek Catholic than Roman Catholic, so H-015 drops. The coordinator's point that the folder is called Leads is fair, and H-012 comes down with it.

title: Belža, Greek Catholic: a second György Demko and a Mária Hriczko
blurb: Two strips from a baptism register that survives as a later hand copy on a printed Slovak form. Entry 13 of 1895: György, born 29 March and baptised 31 March, son of György Demko, Greek Catholic landholding farmer, and Katalin Jobbágy, of Gönyű (Gyňov), house 24. Entry 33 of 1894: Mária, born and baptised 29 August, daughter of József Hriczko, Greek Catholic cottar, and Erzsébet Kocsis, Roman Catholic, of Szina (Seňa), house 182. The folder is called Duska Baptisms and holds no Duska. These villages lie south of Košice, about 80 km west of Senné and Viszoka, in a different county. The father in 1895 shares a name and a rite with György Demkó of Viszoka but has a different wife, so the working view is two separate Demko families (H-016). The useful by-product is entry 33: a daughter of a Greek Catholic father and Roman Catholic mother in a Greek Catholic book, which weakens the coordinator's argument that a Demko daughter of the Viszoka couple had to be baptised Roman Catholic. This batch also takes in the Places agent's first findings, which lift H-007 to supported and raise H-005 and H-010. Six more people are held as unplaced candidates. Nothing is added to the direct line.

title: Ledger v2, the duska.si plan and the Site agent's notes
blurb: No new files. Read ledger v2, the plan for the public site and proof chain, and the Site agent's notes. Applied here: the stamping workflow is added unchanged, so every batch commit is hashed and anchored; hypotheses carry the coordinator's question numbers; documents carry their checksums; a decisions list and a search log now exist. Two rulings changed the board. Labels and filing habits count only as priors, so the B-004 moves on H-012 and H-013 that leaned on the owner's choice of files are undone. Claims resting on context without the record in hand are capped at 70, which trims H-007, H-010 and H-016. The search log answers the coordinator's open question about two early fetch calls to Kevin's own site: this agent's notes from the time record both as blocked. Kevin also gave a new instruction: everything this agent receives comes from his Duska folder, and people in it who are not Duskas are to be worked up with the other agents. Nine more named people from the first three folders are now indexed, each with the agent who should place them. Later the same night Kevin closed Folder 1 for now and allowed one research pass on the surnames, on condition that nothing he has written is opened. That pass was started and its results will be logged as leads in a later batch.

title: Research pass on the surnames and villages
blurb: No new files. The research pass Kevin allowed has reported, and its findings are logged as leads, not as findings. The one that matters most for the Duska line: the Iňačovce municipal website lists a Dúška family among the village's 18th-century households. That is a website, not a record, but it points at Iňačovce and not Senné as the older home of the name, so H-004 drops. On the Demko side the church geography is now sourced: Viszoka's Greek Catholics belonged to the Čičarovce Greek Catholic parish, and Csurgovich is a Greek Catholic clerical family, so H-015 (that the 1882 book is Roman Catholic) falls to 20. Linguists list Hreško and Hricko as separate surnames. No emigration record for a Duska or Demko from these villages was found, and no Demko in any list for Senné or Iňačovce. The report says nothing written by Kevin was met or used. It also discloses that one sub-search queried his connected Gmail for three terms and found nothing; that was not requested and has been reported.

title: Čičarovce baptisms: the Demkos of Viszoka, 1831 to 1883
blurb: Twenty strips from one parish book, filed by the owner under Duska Baptisms. None names a Duska. Fourteen are Demko baptisms at Viszoka, three are children of a Demko mother married to György Tirpák, and three are Kocsis entries with no stated link to either line. One file is a second copy of the 1882 strip from Folder 2. Read together they rebuild two households. György Demkó and Mária Hreskó: a daughter Mária born and dead in 1857, twins Mihály and János in 1873 (both marked with a cross), János in 1875, Borbála in 1879, and the Mihály of 1882. János Demkó and his wife Szlekár, next door at Viszoka 120 in 1879: Anna, Erzsébet, János (who lived twelve days) and Zsuzsánna in 1883. A generation back, two or three fathers named György Demko were baptising children at Viszoka in the 1830s. The folder settles which book this is: the 1870s entries name the officiant as the Greek Catholic pastor of Csicser, and the priest of 1882 signs again in 1883 as János Csurgovich, so H-015 is refuted. It also all but rules out Mária Hreskó as the mother of Ahn 9: she was already a mother in 1857. No Maria Demko of the right age is in the folder. Two further candidates for her father go on the board, and the direct line is unchanged. One label does not match its strip: the 1872 file called Anna Demko reads Szulák.

title: Ledger v3: cross-review of the Demko repo
blurb: No new files. Read ledger v3 and acted on it. The new rule is cross-review: the folder a record arrived in does not decide whose line it belongs to, so each line agent reads the other's repository at the start of every batch. First pass done on the Demko repository at commit 035aef0. It holds one folder, the 1882 strip both agents already share, and nothing that names or places a Duska. In the other direction the traffic is heavy: two of the folders that reached this agent under Duska labels, Belža and Čičarovce, are Demko material by content. Every document, family group and person from them now carries a route code so the Demko agent can take them, and the Places agent gets the households. The Places agent's first note on Senné was also taken in. It names the parish priest of Senné for 1831 to 1841 as a way to tie the Folder 1 copy-book to that parish; the two countersignatures on the pages in hand give only an abbreviated office and no name, so that test is not met yet. Kevin also stated that his father was born in Montréal, which places Stefan Duska in that city by 1962. No confidence moved in this batch.

title: The Duska line goes on paper; Iňačovce Greek Catholic, part 1
blurb: Two things in one batch. First, the cross-review found the records this line was waiting for, in the Demko agent's folder. A sealed certificate from the Roman Catholic parish of Senné, issued in 1947, gives entry 43 of 1929: Štefan, son of Michal Duska, Roman Catholic cottar of Senné, and Maria Demko, Greek Catholic, of Iňačovce, living at Senné 160. A gravestone in Montréal reads Mary Demko, 1906 to 1950, wife of Mike Duska, and a deed of 1966 has Mike Duska declare that he married once and that she died on 9 September 1950. Ahn 4 and Ahn 8 are now documented, not just stated. Štefan was born in Slovakia, so the opening guess that he was born in Canada is refuted; so are four guesses about Maria's parents, since the Demko agent's 1906 civil record names them as Mihály Demkó and Mária Kocsis. That also explains the Kocsis entries in the owner's folders. Second, eleven strips from the Iňačovce Greek Catholic register, 1816 to 1889, covering Jesztreb, Szenna and Solymos: three Krak families, four Demko entries, one Kocsis, and one that matters most here. In 1877 a János Du[s]ko of Szenna 72 and his wife Mari Csizmár, Greek Catholic, baptised a daughter Anna. If the name is Dusko it is the first Duska in the archive outside the 1929 entry, but the third letter can be read as s or n and nothing yet ties house 72 to Michal.

title: Ledger v8: who is living, reused names, provenance
blurb: No new files. Read ledger versions 4 to 8 and the coordinator's method note on epidemics and reused names, and applied them. Kevin has told the coordinator that Štefan Duska, known as Steve, died in 2018, so his full dates from the 1947 certificate are now shown: born 21 October 1929, baptised 26 October. Kevin's father is of unknown status and is shown by name and year only. The method note warns that a baptism is not an identity, because the name of a dead child was often given to a later one. The folders already show it: György Demkó and Mária Hreskó named twins Mihály and János in 1873, both marked with a cross, then a János in 1875 and a Mihály in 1882. So the Mihály of 1882, the man now taken as Maria Demko's father, was the second of his name. The burial registers are not in hand, so that link is marked as an unresolved necronym risk and stays capped at 70; the age on the 1906 civil record, 24, fits the 1882 child and not the 1873 one. The same rule turns three Demko fathers of the 1830s into a hypothesis of one man with three wives. The Demko agent has now read the same Čičarovce strips independently; the two readings differ on one rite mark of 1857, and this agent has moved to its reading. Every document now carries a provenance block, mostly the word unknown. Batches carry their commit time in UTC.

title: Iňačovce Greek Catholic, part 2: Kocsis at Solymos, Krak and Demko at Jesztreb
blurb: Eleven more strips from the same book, 1843 to 1889, and no Duska among them. Four are Kocsis baptisms at Solymos, the village and surname of Maria Demko's mother. A clear entry of 1877 fixes the couple met in part 1: János Kocsis, Greek Catholic, and Anna Kováts, Roman Catholic, at Solymos 13, with a second daughter named Anna two years after the first. A second couple, Mihály Kocsis and Mária Knyezső, has a daughter at Solymos 19 in 1889; either couple could be the parents of the Mária Kocsis born there about 1886, and that is the Demko agent's question to settle. An older Pál Kocsis baptised two daughters named Borbála in 1843 and 1846 by two different wives. Three strips extend the Demko household at Jesztreb: Michael Demko and Maria Lazár had twins János and György in 1877 and an Erzsébet in 1884 who died at six months, and Zsuzsi Demko, wife of János Szmeriga, was already bearing children in 1845. Three are Krak entries from Jesztreb. One godmother to the Demko twins is read as Anna Krak[o], the first sign of why Krak is in this archive, and it points to the Demko side. One strip, labelled Nyemcsik, is a Szeman child from Nagy Szeretva with no visible link to anything. One strip includes the register's printed headings.

title: Ledger v10: reused names are craft knowledge
blurb: No new files. Read ledger v10. It corrects version 9, which for a few minutes recorded a belief of Kevin's about reused names in this family; what he said is only that a genealogist of this region would know the custom. This agent went straight from version 8 to version 10 and never read version 9, so nothing here rested on it. The reused names on this board are read from the strips themselves: a Mihály and a János to György Demkó and Mária Hreskó in 1873 and again in 1882 and 1875, an Anna to János Kocsis in 1875 and 1877, a Borbála to Pál Kocsis in 1843 and 1846, an András to János Kóreny and Mária Krak in 1844 and 1852. They stand as findings on that evidence. No entry changed.

title: Iňačovce Greek Catholic, parts 3 to 5: the Duskos appear, and one of them turns out to be a Danko
blurb: Thirty-six strips close the folder at 58 files, and the Duska surname is finally on the page. A Mihály Dusko, Greek Catholic, and his Roman Catholic wife baptised a son János at Szenna in 1846. A generation later György Dusko and Mária Hornyák had a Mihail in 1869, a Maria at Szenna 31 in 1874 and a György at Solymos 31 in 1877; a Mária Dusko and an Anna Duska were mothers at Jesztreb and Solymos in 1894, the second of them Reformed. None of these is yet tied to Michal Duska of Senné, and they are Greek Catholic men where he is Roman Catholic. The same strips undo a reading from part 1. Set beside the clerk's own 'Dusko Gyuri', the father at Szenna 72 in 1877 is a Danko, a separate family that is written plainly in 1896, so the two hypotheses built on him are refuted. The Krak puzzle is solved in outline: the owner's 'maybe incest' couple, Mihály Krak and Anna Krak, are Mihály Bodnár and his wife, shown by their godparents and by a later Slovak note that the son's correct name is Bodnár. For the Demko agent there is a Mária Kocsis born at Solymos 19 in February 1887, the best candidate so far for Maria Demko's mother, and the Jesztreb Demko household now runs from 1864 to 1885.

title: Ledger v13: the unclassified folder will come through a sorter
blurb: No new files. Read ledger v13; versions 11 and 12 were never read by this agent, and v13 replaces what they said. The owner has one more folder, which he calls 'AAAA Unclassified'. It is mixed, and parts of it concern lines that are outside this experiment. A separate sorting agent, working elsewhere, is to divide it into piles in a private repository, and this agent may open two of them only: the pile marked for the Duska line and the pile marked for both lines. The pile a file sits in is the sorter's label and counts as a prior, like the owner's own folder names; it raises no confidence. The rule is now in the protocol. Nothing has been taken yet: the ledger shows the sorter as not started, and this session was refused read access to the private repository, which is the owner's to grant. A check of this repository for anything about the lines outside the experiment found nothing. The cross-review of the Demko repository found four cards of soldiers named Demko who died between 1915 and 1918 and three strips from a 'Demko Hints' folder; none names a Duska. The Demko agent now holds two rival Kocsis couples as parents of Maria Demko's mother and asks for a baptism of a Mária Kocsis at Solymos between 1885 and 1887. One was sent to it in the last batch, born at house 19 in February 1887, which is the house of one of its two couples.

title: Ledger v14: blind lines and open lines; the Places agent names the volumes
blurb: No new files. Read ledger v14. The project is to cover the owner's whole tree in time, and not all of it is a blind test. The Duska and Demko lines stay blind and are scored against his own tree. A second kind of agent now works beside them with everything he knows, on a question that lies outside this line, and a sorter divides his mixed folder. This agent may read none of their chats, notes or folders, and that is now rule 23 of the protocol. One thing is reported to the coordinator: the memory index that the project shows to every chat carries a one-line description of an older note that names a family outside this line. The note itself was not opened here and nothing from it is in this repository. The private repository is still closed to this session, so the two piles meant for this agent have not been taken. The useful news is from the Places agent, which has read the Prešov state archive's catalogue of church registers. The 58 Iňačovce strips come from four numbered volumes covering 1811 to 1898. The Senné Roman Catholic baptisms survive there only from 1866, in one volume, and that is the book in which Michal Duska's own baptism should be found; the same parish's burials are in two more. The Reformed families of Iňačovce had a register of their own, which is where the Reformed Anna Duska of 1894 should be sought. These are logged as leads. The Places agent found no documented custom in these villages of entering a man under his wife's surname, so the Krak and Bodnár identification stays at 70. One later note on a strip is now transcribed as written: 'Zomrela 18. augusta 1934', she died on 18 August 1934.

title: Ledgers v15 and v16; the first file from the sorter's piles is somebody else's family tree
blurb: The owner gave this session read access to the private repository, and the two piles meant for this agent were read at once. The pile for the Duska line is empty. The shared pile holds one file: a printed family-tree chart of a family named Javor, with the Slovak word for 'preview' stamped across it. No Duska can be read anywhere on it. One ancestor can be read in part, a woman called Mary Danko or Demko, born in 1906 and dead in 1991, whose parents are placed at Vysoká nad Uhom, the village of the Demko baptisms in an earlier folder. She is not Maria Demko of this line, who was also born in 1906 but died at Montréal in 1950; the two must not be merged. Whether her name is Demko at all is raised as a question for the Demko agent. The chart shows living people with their birth dates, so the image is not published here: only its name and checksum are. Ledgers v15 and v16 are read too. Version 16 brings the coordinator's tables level with the boards and asks each blind agent what it can see of the owner's memory notes; the answer is in the note to the coordinator. Version 15 rules how the wife of Štefan Duska will be entered when a record of their marriage arrives: her name and the marriage, nothing of her own family. The cross-review settled five small differences with the Demko agent. Four go its way after a second look at the strips: a house number at Jesztreb is 28, not 38; a birth of 1866 is the 14th or 15th of March; a Kocsis baptism belongs to November 1847; and an 'unfinished' row of 1870 is the first attempt at an entry made properly three lines later, so one child, Anna, born in January 1871, where two were counted.

title: The Reformed book of Iňačovce: a village full of Duskas, and two boys named Mihály
blurb: Forty-five strips arrived in four parts, a whole folder the owner calls 'Inacovce - Reformed Catholic'. There is no such church. The entries are from a Reformed, that is Calvinist, register for Solymos, the Hungarian name of Iňačovce: its ministers sign as preacher and Reformed pastor, and it runs from 1825 to 1921. This is where the Duska name lives. Thirty-two of the strips name a Duska, against a handful in the Greek Catholic book. The oldest household is András Duska and Borbála Pluchta, with six children from 1829 to 1843; beside them a János Duska and Anna Hura; a generation on, János Dusko and Anna Kitko with six children from 1863 to 1876 and Mihály Dusko and Ilona Mihalko at house 33; then two Györgys, a second Mihály, and Duska daughters marrying out. Names are reused as children die: two Susannas, two Jánoses, two Györgys. Two boys could be Michal Duska of this line. One Mihály was born at Solymos 44 in January 1893. The other is on a strip the owner filed under another child's name: a Mihály born in October, probably of 1902, to György Duska, a labourer, at a place written 'Bradenville', and copied into the home book from a certificate. If that is the town in Pennsylvania, the family was in America and came back. Neither boy is attached. Both are Reformed, and the one record that names Michal's church calls him a Roman Catholic of Senné. So the hypothesis that he was born at Senné is lowered, not dropped, and each boy becomes a rival to it. The twelve strips labelled 'Nyemcsik' all read Knyezso, the surname of a woman on the Demko side, and go to the Demko agent.

title: The owner has no more folders: the held requests are released
blurb: No new files. The owner says that the folders sent so far are all he has for this line. Six folders came from him directly, 136 files; one more file came through the sorter and three were taken from the Demko agent's folder. All 140 are read into documents. The line stands at four generations. Štefan Duska, born at Senné in 1929, and his parents Michal Duska and Maria Demko are documented by a 1947 certificate, a gravestone and a deed. Nothing in the archive records Michal's own birth, his parents or his marriage, and that is where the rebuild stops. What it has instead is the surname in three churches around him and two unattached boys named Mihály Duska in the Reformed book. Under the working rules, requests for more material were held until the folders ran out. They are now put to the owner, ten in all, ranked by how much each would settle. First is Michal's own baptism or his marriage entry, either of which would name his parents. Second is the full row for the boy born at 'Bradenville'. The data is not frozen for comparison: the owner's unsorted folder is still being divided by the sorter, and anything it sends to this agent's piles will be read as it comes.

title: Four Latin entries from the Greek Catholic church of Prešov
blurb: The last batch said the owner had no more folders. He had: this one, and another that follows. So that statement is corrected here and the requests stay open. This folder is four strips from the Greek Catholic parish of Eperjes, today Prešov, the bishop's town about 60 kilometres west of Senné. None names a Duska. Two are the same baptism of 1822 written twice, once as a Latin sentence and once in ruled columns: Andreas, son of Andreas Nyemcsik, a clerk of the town. He is a real Nyemcsik; the twelve strips the owner filed under that name in the Reformed folder all read Knyezso. One strip of 1804 is a Catharina, daughter of Joannes and Eva Kocsis. The fourth, of 1809, is the son of the Very Reverend Stephanus Demko, Greek Catholic parish priest of a village called Körösfő. A priest named Demko is worth the Demko agent's time, and the Kocsis entry goes to it too. Nothing here is tied to either line by a record; what the owner saw in these four is not known. No confidence moved. Curiosities: 2

title: The Senné Roman Catholic book, part 1: Duskas in Michal's own church, and a household with a gap where he should be
blurb: Read ledger v18 (v17 was never seen here; v18 carries it). Sixteen strips open the folder this rebuild has been waiting for: the Roman Catholic register of Senné, the church and village that the 1929 certificate gives for Michal Duska. Part 1 covers only the strips the owner named Andras to Anna, so Michal's own entry, if he has it, is still to come. What is here is his kind of family. Georgius Duska, a Roman Catholic cottar at house 6, and his Greek Catholic wife Anna Krak baptised a daughter in 1866 and a son Andreas in 1868; a later hand notes that the son died in August 1940. That one line explains two things: why Krak baptisms sit in the owner's Duska folders, and who the next man may be. An András Duska, farm servant and then cottar at house 73, baptised six children from 1893 to 1907, losing four of them, with no child recorded between 1899 and 1907. A Mihály born in that gap would be the right age, church, village and standing. It is raised as the leading hypothesis for Michal's parents, at 35, and not attached. A second household, György Duska the younger, a miller at house 1, is the rival. The two Reformed boys of the last folder drop back. Also here: a Roman Catholic János Demko at Senné in 1900, sent to the Demko agent; two real Nyemcsik entries; and one entry the owner saved twice. Three new working rules from the ledger are taken in: no DNA material is read, curiosities are logged in every batch, and the ledger is read at the start of each. Curiosities: 5

title: The Senné Roman Catholic book, part 2: eleven girls named Anna, and a second miller
blurb: Read ledger v19. Eleven more strips from the Senné Roman Catholic register, and every child on them is an Anna: the owner's files are in alphabetical order and have not yet reached M. So there is still no entry for a Mihály, and the question of Michal Duska's parents stands where the last batch left it. Two strips touch the Duska name. A miller called János, of house 115, baptised a daughter in 1900; the owner himself is unsure whether the surname is Duska or Drska, and so is this reading. If it is Duska, Senné had two Duska millers within five years. And a Roman Catholic Anna Duska was the wife of János Marczinyik at Solymos in 1876. The rest are the other names the owner gathers: six Nyemcsik strips, showing at least three men called János Nyemcsik; three Kocsis strips, sent to the Demko agent; and one child filed as Nyemcsik who is a Murnyik with a Nyemcsik godfather. The husband of Mária Nyemcsik turns out to be the sexton of the last batch, a farmer fourteen years earlier, spelled a third way. The strips also narrow when the village was renamed Ungszenna: after June 1903 and by May 1906. From the ledger: the stamping file is replaced with its second version, and the question of Michal's parents now has a number of its own. Curiosities: 2

title: The rest of the Senné book, and a marriage from the sorter's pile: two boys named Mihály, and one family all the way round
blurb: Read ledger v19. Sixty-eight more images finish the owner's run of the Senné Roman Catholic register, from Borbála to Zsuzsanna, and four files arrived in this agent's pile in the private repository. One more file, a text document the owner wrote about these baptisms, is held unopened under the blind rule. The book has two boys named Mihály Duska of the right age. One was born on 6 December 1896 to Mihály Duska, the village miller. The other was born on 3 July 1903 to András Duska, a cottar, and a mother entered as Anna Nyemecz, in the gap the last batches pointed to. Neither has a death written beside him, in a book that notes deaths freely. The pile then supplied what the strips could not. A marriage entry of 18 January 1892 joins András Duska, aged 24, son of György Duska and Anna Krak, to Anna Nyemcsik, aged 19, daughter of János Nyemcsik and Erzsébet Hresko. Her mother is twice written 'Hresko, otherwise Minarcsin', which is why the priest called the daughter Anna Minarcsin for seven years: one wife, not two, and thirteen children. It also explains at last why the owner gathers Nyemcsik and Krak records. So if Michal is the boy of 1903, his four grandparents are in hand. That 'if' is not settled. The 1903 boy is put at 55, the miller's son at 22, and nobody above Michal is entered on the tree; one record with his age would decide it. Also here: the older György Duska had a second wife; the doubtful 'Duska or Drska' miller is a Duska; a screenshot gives the first archive reference for the book; a burial page takes the Reformed Duskas back to a Pál born about 1770; and the first page of the volume lists every priest of Senné since the church was 'recovered from the Calvinists' in 1718. Curiosities: 10

title: Putting things in order: a folder closed, two files kept shut, and three more from the pile
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. Asked whether the Senné folder was complete and whether to open his own summary of it, the owner said to judge as this agent saw fit. Two judgments follow. The Senné Roman Catholic folder is closed at 95 files: its names run from A to Z. And the owner's summary stays unopened. It is his own account of these baptisms, the very thing this rebuild is to be measured against, and reading it could not be undone. Three more files had reached the pile in the private repository. One is a page from an online family tree, which the sorter had held back and the owner moved across. It is kept shut for the same reason: a tree page with no sources proves nothing, and it may be his tree. Its file name is logged as something known beforehand. The second is the owner's census find, at last: a photograph of a computer screen showing a household of five, headed by a György Duska born about 1820 at Solymos, with a son György born about 1846 'working beside his father' and an infant Mihály. They are Greek Catholic, the Iňačovce family of an earlier folder, and not Michal's people on the present reading. The image is too blurred to give years to the digit and shows no village or archive. The third is a nine-line newspaper report of January 1911: a hotel gas plant exploded at Niobrara, Nebraska, and an Annie Duska was among the four dead. Nothing ties her to this family. The status file and the protocol's summary of where the line stands are rewritten. No confidence about Michal moved. Curiosities: 2

title: One strip from Sztára: an Anna Krak of 1848, and a rival for her
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The owner sent a folder of one strip, marked full, named 'Baptisms (Final) Stare'. It is a Hungarian baptism entry, the first under the heading for 1848: Anna, daughter of János Krak, Roman Catholic, and Mária [Z]ebro, of Sztára, a village about 26 km from Senné. The folder's name says the owner takes this for the baptism of Anna Krak, the Greek Catholic wife of György Duska the elder, and that he considers the search finished. That is logged as something known beforehand and given no weight. On the evidence here it is the weaker of two candidates. An earlier folder holds another Anna Krak born the same year, in October, at Jesztreb, 4 km from Senné and in a Greek Catholic book, also the daughter of a János Krak. Nothing in the archive says which girl, if either, married György Duska; her marriage entry would. So two hypotheses are raised: the Sztára girl at 20 in 100 and the Jesztreb girl at 35. She is in Michal Duska's line only if he is the boy of 1903, so none of this moves the main question. The Places agent is asked which church's book this strip comes from. The owner also said a 'Duska Census' folder is beginning and that his word files may be inaccurate; that is for the next batch. Curiosities: 2

title: The urbarial tables: Duskas at Solymos about 1770, and none at Senné
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The owner opened a new folder, 'Duska Census', with eight images of the urbarial tables of Maria Theresa's time: printed forms, filled in by hand, that list each landlord's serfs and cottars and what they owed. He dates them 1767; the images carry no date. They are the oldest records in the archive by sixty years. Three pages cover Solymos (Iňačovce) from first serf to final total, so every household head of the village is in hand. Two are certainly Duskas. Mihály Duska was a serf with a full holding of 20 holds under the lord Sándor Szirmay, owing 52 days of labour a year with his animals, a florin, firewood, yarn, butter, poultry and eggs. György Duska, under the same lord, was a cottar with a house and no land. The owner's file name puts a third man there, 'Andref Duska'; the name on the page is read here as [B]utka, with doubt, and that is raised as a hypothesis at 55 in 100 that he is not a Duska. Two pages cover Szenna (Senné): 25 of its 26 serfs and all its cottars, and no Duska among them. A public archive portal's own head counts match the images to the man, which is how the lists are known to be complete. So about 1770 the name was at Solymos and, all but certainly, not at Senné. A new hypothesis says the Senné Duskas came from Solymos, at 35 in 100: it fits the map, but the later Solymos Duskas are Reformed and Greek Catholic and the Senné ones Roman Catholic. One page each for Csicser and Viszoka goes to the Demko agent: a Joannes Kocsis, and Michael Demko, a full serf of the convent of Lelesz. A word-processor file, a guide to the urbarium, came with the images. It is the owner's own writing, and he says such files may be inaccurate; it is held unopened like the others. The folder stays open. Curiosities: 3

title: A cemetery record matched to a Senné baptism; every Duska is tracked
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. Two things. First, the owner said of the woman killed in Nebraska in 1911 that she is a Duska and that Duskas are tracked. That is taken as a rule: every bearer of the name is followed, kin or not, and kinship still has to be shown by a record. Her clipping is now read whole. A search by place and event, leaving the surname out so that nothing of the owner's would come back, found a Nebraska paper that calls her 'Ann Duseka, a cook' at the hotel. So her name is spelled two ways, and a hypothesis that she belongs to this family is raised at 5 in 100. Second, a new file in the sorter's pile: a printout from a cemetery's records system, in French, for a 'Mikalis' Duska, born 28 November 1890, husband of Anna Hancosek, plot FT 01965. The Senné register read two batches ago has a Miklós Duska born on exactly that day at house 6, son of György Duska the younger. That the two are one man is held at 70 in 100, the cap without an archive reference. He is not Michal: a different name, a different wife, and Michal was alive a year after this record's date. But it puts a Duska of that one Senné house under a French-language cemetery record, as would be expected of kin of Mike Duska of Montréal. The record's other dates are a system's stand-ins and give nobody's age, so the main question does not move. The Demko repository was read at its latest commit: nothing new for this line. Curiosities: 3

title: The Solymos census: four Duska households, three churches
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The owner sent the second part of the census folder, marked full: four household sheets of the Hungarian census of 1869 for Solymos, as photographs of a computer screen, with small screenshots of each. The full-size photographs came inside an archive file, which was unpacked in an empty folder. Read from the images first, the sheets give every Duska household of the village with years of birth. András, born 1797, Reformed, a farmer, with a Roman Catholic wife born at Senné. János, born 1810, Reformed, a farmer, with sons Mihály and György. János, born 1835, Reformed, a servant lodging with his wife and small son in another man's house. And György, born 1820, Greek Catholic, with his married son György, born 1846, and a grandson Mihály born that year. Three of the four match families already built from the Reformed register, which raises the hypothesis that those families are one from 55 to 65. One earlier hypothesis is refuted: the younger György was thought to be a son of a Mihály Dusko, and the sheet says he works beside his father, György. Three new hypotheses cover two second marriages and a possible common father, Pál, who died in 1838. None of these people is Michal's ancestor on present evidence: the Roman Catholic Duskas are at Senné, and the Senné sheets are not in the folder. They are now asked for, since they would say where the two György Duskas of Senné were born. Six files are not published. Four are 'family group records', pages compiled from the owner's own tree, and were not opened. One is a transcription made for him by a third party; it was opened only after this reading was written, agrees on every Duska, and differs on five other names, which are given side by side. The folder stays open. Curiosities: 3

title: Two maps of Ung county and a guide to the census of 1921
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The owner opened a '1921 Census Folder' with two maps and a guide; no census page yet. The first map, of the 1890s, shows Solymos and Szenna four kilometres apart with marsh between them and a district boundary running through the gap, so records kept by district hold the two villages in different bundles. The second, of 1915, prints the Magyarised names: Ungszenna, and Magasrév where the older map has Viszoka. Someone has added a coloured square to every village on it, with no key; they look like the main language of each village, and that reading is this agent's guess. The guide is the owner's machine translation of an archive portal's page. It is about a kind of record, not about the family, so it was read: the Czechoslovak census of 1921 for the region survives nearly whole at the Berehove archive and is online, and its household forms give each person's date and place of birth. That matters more than anything else in the folder. If the Senné forms exist, one of them lists Michal Duska as a young man in his father's house, and the main question is answered. It is now the first request. No confidence moved. Curiosities: 2

title: The emigration of 1937, in the family's own papers; and a document for the link to Kevin's father
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. Nine files had reached the sorter's pile. Eight are photographs of one set of papers from 1937, kept in the family. In September of that year Mike Duska, of 1196a St. George Street, Montréal, applied to Ottawa for his wife Maria and son Stefan to be admitted, and paid $178.50 for their passage. In October the court at Michalovce consented that the boy might emigrate with his mother to his father, Michal Duško, in Canada. Maria's emigrant passport gives her birth as 22 August 1906 at Iňačovce and carries her photograph with the boy. On 8 November she signed a contract in Prague for the train to Antwerp and the ship Montrose, sailing on the 11th for Montréal. Two hypotheses fall: Štefan did not leave after the war, and his father did not wait until then to send for him. He left at eight. A second kind of record is the ninth file, a Québec declaration of marriage of 1984, which names the father of Kevin's father as Steve Duska, born in Czechoslovakia. That link rested on Kevin's word until now. Its image is held and most of its fields are withheld, since they concern people of unknown living status and lines outside this experiment. One photograph is published cropped for the same reason. What the papers do not give is Michal's age: he is named four times and never described. So the main question stands where it was. But the papers show where his age must be written down: he reached Canada before his family, most likely between 1929 and 1931, and his own passenger list will state it. That is now the first request. Curiosities: 5

title: Where the 1937 papers were found
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. No new file. The owner said where the 1937 emigration papers came from: he found them himself, as originals, in the basement of his grandfather Steve, who is the boy named in them. That is entered on each of the eight documents as their history of keeping, and the Demko agent and the coordinator are told. It is a statement about where paper was kept, from the person who found it, and it strengthens the papers as evidence. It adds no fact about the people in them, and no confidence moved. Curiosities: 1

title: The 1984 marriage form released in part
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. No new file. The Québec declaration of marriage of 1984 was held last batch because it shows people whose status was not known. The owner has now said two things: his mother, the bride, is dead, so there is no need to hold on her account; and he does not know whether his father is alive. So the form is released in part. Shown: the marriage of Kevin Duska and Lyne Lefebvre at the Palais de Justice in Montréal on 11 October 1984, her birth in Montréal in 1964, and the groom's father, Steve Duska, born in Czechoslovakia, who signed as witness. Blacked out on the published copy: the groom's day and month of birth, the couple's address and his signature, since he may be living; and the bride's parents, the groom's mother, the second witness and the official, about whom nothing new was said. Nothing changes on the tree but a sentence on Kevin's father. Curiosities: 0

title: A census sheet of 1930 from Beša: the Schwarcz household
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The owner sent a folder of one file, marked whole: a household sheet of the Czechoslovak census of 1930 for Beša, a village in the Veľké Kapušany district. It lists the family of Ignác Schwarcz, a Jewish merchant born in 1865: his wife Fanny, their son Lipót and his wife Hermin, and three grandchildren born from 1921 to 1926, each with a full date of birth. No Duska and no Demko is on it. Why it sits among the Duska census files is not said. The one Schwarz in this archive is Erzsébet Schwarz, the Catholic wife of György Duska the younger of Senné, and nothing here connects her with this house; the filing is logged as something known beforehand and no hypothesis is raised on a surname alone. What the sheet does show is what a 1930 form holds: exact birth dates, the year a person came to the village, and the home commune. A sheet like it for Senné would list Maria Duska and her son a year after his birth, and would say whether Michal was at home or already gone. That is added to the requests. Curiosities: 2

title: The census of 1930 names Michal's parents
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The owner sent eleven deliveries of the Czechoslovak census of 1930 at once, 81 images. This batch reads the two for Senné, 35 images, and one file from the sorter's pile. The other 46 images are logged with checksums as received and not yet read. The Senné sheets answer the main question. House 145, on the night of 1 December 1930: Andrej Duška, born 24 November 1868; his wife Anna, born 24 August 1872, married 18 January 1892; their son Juraj; their daughter-in-law Maria, Greek Catholic, born at Iňačovce; and their grandson Štefan, born 23 October 1929. The marriage date and Anna's birthday are those of András Duska and Anna Nyemcsik in records read earlier. Their one son named Mihály was baptised on 3 July 1903. So Michal Duska was that boy, and the rival, the miller's son of 1896, is ruled out. The pile file agrees: a passenger list has Michal Duska of Senné, aged 26, crossing to Canada with Mikulas Duska, 39, and carries the immigration file number of the 1937 letter to Mike Duska of Montréal. The ages put the crossing between November 1929 and July 1930. András and Anna go onto the tree as Michal's parents. The generation above them stays a hypothesis at 70, because the 1892 marriage image has no archive reference. The owner's second pass shows where the sheets are kept: the Slovak National Archive, on its public portal, box 0311. The census also gives the date of Michal and Maria's marriage, 30 January 1927, and shows three Duska houses where the husband was away. Five sheets are held because they show a child born after 1926; their contents are abstracted with years only. Curiosities: 4

title: Senné in the census of 1940: names only
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. Twelve screen captures of the Slovak census of December 1940 for Senné, and five word files. The archive's portal shows the 1940 sheets with everything but the names blacked out, so only names can be read. They are enough for one thing. At house 11 the wife of Mikuláš Duška is entered with her maiden name, Hankoščáková, and Mikuláš himself is listed on the back among those away from home. The French cemetery record read four batches ago names the spouse of a Duska born on Mikuláš's birthday as 'Hancosek'. It is the same surname. Her given name differs, Mária here and Anna there, so the identification stays at 70. House 14 holds a widow alone, and house 73 the family of Jozef Duška, now with a second Jozef and his wife. One sheet the owner marked 'maybe Demko' is from a different Senné in the south of Slovakia and reads Semko. Five sheets are held because they name people who may be living. The five word files are the owner's own lists of households drawn up for a transcriber; they are held unopened. Still unread from this morning: 46 sheets of the 1930 census for nine other villages and six files in the sorter's pile. Curiosities: 2

title: Ten held census captures released
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. No new file. Ten captures of the 1930 and 1940 census sheets for Senné were held because they show people born after 1926 whose status was not known. Told this, the owner answered 'all dead'. The ten are released on his word. They were already public on the Slovak National Archive's portal. The statement is read narrowly: it covers the people on those ten sheets, not his father, and not the people still blacked out on the 1984 marriage form, about whom he is asked. Nothing on the tree changes. Curiosities: 0

title: Michal's death, Štefan's marriage, and a second son
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The six remaining files of the sorter's pile. A death notice from The Montreal Star: Mike Duska, Sr., died at the Montreal General Hospital on 31 January 1974, aged 71, husband of the late Mary Demko, father of Steve and Mike, grandfather of Kevin, buried in Côte-des-Neiges cemetery from the Slovak church of St. Cyril and Method. So Michal Duska's life now has both ends: Senné, 3 July 1903, and Montréal, 31 January 1974. The notice shows a second son, Mike, born in Canada, of whom nothing else is entered. A parish extract of Štefan's baptism, issued at Senné on 1 October 1955, repeats the 1947 certificate and gives the godmother plainly as Zuzanna Bandura, born Hankoščák. It was ordered for his wedding: the provincial registration shows Stephen Duska, superintendent, marrying Joan Teresa Leonard at St. Dominic's Church, Montréal, on 26 November 1955. She is entered as the paternal grandmother by name only, as the coordinator ruled, and the image is held. A 1973 marriage form for a Mike Duska is held unopened, since both parties may be living. A small second copy of the 1890 baptism of Miklós Duska and a duplicate of the cemetery record complete the pile. A new hypothesis puts that cemetery record at Côte-des-Neiges, at 60 in 100. Curiosities: 2

title: The census of 1930 in nine other villages
blurb: Read ledger v19, unchanged. The 46 census sheets left unread two batches ago: Čičarovce, Iňačovce, Maťovce, a village the owner calls Mogyoros, Palín, Pavlovce, Veľké Kapušany, Veľké Slemence and Vysoká. They were read quickly, from reduced images and for the left-hand columns only, and each is abstracted, not transcribed. One sheet is a Duska: Barbora Dušková, a Reformed widow alone at Iňačovce 28, married 1887 and widowed on 14 January 1914, probably the wife of the Reformed Mihály Duska of the 1890s. Everything else belongs to the other line or to neither. The find of the batch is for the Demko agent. At Iňačovce 117 lives Michal Demko, born at Vysoká in August 1882: the father of Maria Demko. He has a second wife, married in 1919, a son of 1911 by the first, and in the house a widowed mother-in-law named Kočišová, born 1863, who may be the mother of his first wife. At Vysoká a Ján Demko born in April 1875 is very probably his brother. Eighteen Iňačovce sheets are of the Knyezso family, written Kňežo, and the rest are Kocsis, Hreško and four Jewish households named Schwarz, which the owner gathered across five villages for a reason not stated. Three of his labels misname the household, one of them a Danko filed as a Demko. 18 sheets are held, either for a child born after 1926 or because their lower rows were not read. Curiosities: 3

title: Ledger v20; the second son; a guide opened
blurb: Read ledger v20. It records the line as moved two generations and the main question as solved, and it rules on the owner's own files: anything he compiled about the family stays shut until the comparison; a guide to a kind of record may be read; a transcription made for him by someone else may be read after one's own. So the urbarium guide held since batch 25 was opened. It is a copy of a third party's article on the census of 1767 with translations of the column headings, and names nobody. The other nine of his files stay shut. The owner then said that 'Mike Jr', the second son named in the 1974 death notice, has died. The ledger had ruled his 1973 marriage record held and unopened because his status was unknown; with a death stated, that ground is gone and the record was opened. Michael Duska, born in Montréal on 1 December 1938, inspection manager, married at St-Alphonse d'Youville on 8 December 1973. The bride may be living and is given by name and year only; the image stays held. The form does not name his parents, so that he is the son of Michal and Maria is a hypothesis at 75 in 100. It also types his ethnic origin as 'Hindu' and his father's birthplace as 'India', which is a clerk's error. The death notice is now shown as a crop of the notice alone, without the page that carries the owner's account name. Curiosities: 1

title: Four great-great-great-grandparents entered; the 1906 birth record read
blurb: The owner asked for the latest ledger to be read and acted on. It is still version 20, which was taken in last batch for its two new rulings; this batch works through the rest of it. First, the ledger points to the Places agent's entry for the Senné register, which gives the archive's volume numbers. That supplies what was missing for the marriage of 18 January 1892: the entry is in hand as an image with page and entry number, the volume is no. 1092 at the Prešov state archive, and the census of 1930 gives the same wedding date for Andrej and Anna Duška. The entry names all four of their parents. So the generation above is entered: György Duska the elder and Anna Krak, János Nyemcsik and Erzsébet Hresko, also called Minarcsin. Nothing is known yet of their own births. Second, the ledger told this agent to read the state birth registration of Maria Demko for itself and stop citing it at second hand. It is copied in and read: born at Solymos on 22 August 1906 to Mihály Demkó, 24, and Mária Kocsis, 20. By this agent's own slip the Demko agent's transcription was seen first, so the reading is a check, not an independent one; the two agree. Third, the coordinator's reference numbers are added to seven documents, and its new request, for the original 1929 baptism entry of Štefan, is added to the list. The Demko agent's request that shared files be announced by name and checksum only, without readings, is adopted from now on. Curiosities: 1

title: Ledger v22: what kind of object is each document
blurb: Read ledger v22, and v21 before it. Version 21 is a rewrite that makes the ledger short and adds two rules: the owner's word in this chat beats the ledger, and the coordinator no longer keeps a copy of this board. Its table of who is living counts the villagers on the census sheets as dead on the owner's word, so the eighteen sheets held last time are released. It also says the owner hands over his folders by kind, baptisms, then census, then deaths, then marriages; two requests for marriages and burials are changed from asked-for to waited-for. Version 22 adds one rule of method: before relying on a document, say what kind of object it is from its form. That was done for every paper on the direct line that is not a plain register strip, and for the strips whose church is known only from a folder name, 37 documents in all, each with its form, what does not fit, who made it and where such a paper was kept. Three papers change their name. The Québec forms of 1955, 1973 and 1984, called marriage registrations here until now, are statistical returns that the officiant sent to the government; the act of marriage was the church's or the courthouse's own register, which is not in hand. Nothing they say is withdrawn, but it explains why none names the couple's parents. The 1966 paper is one page of a deed of sale, whatever its label says about a guardianship. The 1906 birth record is a state register entry, and a published account of that series says copies went to the county archive, which raises the county-copy explanation for Uzhhorod to 70. A second look at the 1892 marriage register found the groom's address: Hrabó, the manor farm of Senné. Curiosities: 2

title: The census folder ends: a 1921 sheet that is not a Duska, and fourteen word files
blurb: The owner sent the last part of his census folder, a sub-folder he calls 'Transcarpathian', then fourteen word files, and said the census folder ends here. The one image is a household sheet of the Czechoslovak census of 1921 for Nižní Domanince, a village beside Uzhhorod that Hungarian records call Alsódomonya: house 147, a farm labourer of 25, his wife of 21 and her brother of 17, all Greek Catholic Rusyns. The owner's file name asks 'Dusko or Duska'. The sheet says neither. The surname is written three times and each time it reads Durkota, so this is not a Duska household, and it is logged as a reading that differs from the owner's label (H-072, 90). Of the fourteen word files, eight are lists the owner drew up for a translator and one is his list of villages to search; those nine stay unopened until the comparison, like the five before them. The other five were opened far enough to see what they are. Four hold nothing but web links to the archive portal, one link for every census sheet of Senné, Iňačovce and Seňa in 1930, and one is three lines of search counts. None says anything about the family. The link lists are kept as a lead: with them every household of Senné in 1930 can be read, which is the way to find every Duska there. The folder is closed at 113 documents. Curiosities: 1

title: A new folder: present-day land at Senné, one file, held
blurb: A new folder, 'Duska Contemporary Land', with one file; the owner says it is not exhaustive and that the Places agent may want to know of it. It is a print-out from the Slovak land register made on 11 May 2022: an ownership sheet for Senné, which lists a family house with its yard and a garden, a little over a thousand square metres together, inside the village. The owners are a married couple named Duška, who hold it jointly; nothing is charged against it. The owner's file name calls it a parcel with a number. The number is that of the ownership sheet, and the parcels have other numbers. Both owners were born less than a hundred years ago and nothing says they have died, so under the rules of this experiment the file is held: their given names, birth dates, house number and parcel numbers are not published, and the file name is written with the given name withheld. Whether this household descends from the Duskas of the Senné registers is raised as a question (H-073, 50); surname and village are all that tie them so far. The owner has been asked whether the two are living. Curiosities: 1

title: Deaths begin: nine burials from the Belža parish
blurb: The owner has begun his folder of deaths, as the coordinator's ledger said he would after the census. The first sub-folder, which he marks as full, is nine strips from a burial register he files under the Greek Catholic parish of Belža near Košice, the parish of two baptisms in an earlier folder. Eight are Demkos and their kin and go to the Demko agent. Two of them matter for a rule the coordinator set early. György Demko and Katalin Jobbágy of Gönyű lost a son György to diphtheria in March [1892] and a son János in October; the György baptised in 1895, already on file, is therefore a second child of that name. A gardener named Demko at Csány and Gecse buried two infant daughters called Mária in [1849] and [1850]; a gardener László Demko died at Kenyhec in [1889] aged 80 and may be the same man (H-074, 60). One strip is filed as a Duska: Joannes, called Vanyo, a man 'of Galicia' living at Szina, who died suddenly in May [1863] aged 45. The surname may read Duska or Driska. Seňa is about eighty kilometres from Senné and the man came from over the mountains, so he is indexed, as every bearer of the name is, and not attached (H-075, 85 that he is no kin). The years in square brackets stand only in the owner's file names. Curiosities: 3

title: Eighteen burials from Čičarovce: reused names, three wives, and dates that do not fit the pages
blurb: The second sub-folder of deaths: eighteen strips from the Greek Catholic register of Čičarovce, sixteen of them Demkos of Viszoka and Pálóc and two Kocsis, complete by the owner's word. They are the burials that the baptisms of an earlier folder were waiting for, and all go to the Demko agent. Three things stand out. First, György Demkó, the farmer whose children were baptised from 1857 to 1882, buried a János aged two in December [1872], then the twins Mihály and János at twelve and fifteen days in June 1873, and a Mihály one month old in a May when the family lived at house 121. The Mihály of 1882, who is the Demko line's ancestor, had one brother of his name before him and probably two. Second, three women were buried at Viszoka as the wife of a György Demko within eleven years: Barbara, 25, in [1831]; Ilona, 33, in [1836]; Anna, 37, in [1842]. A György and an Anna had children baptised in [1834] and [1838], so Ilona's husband was another man. The idea of one György with three wives in turn falls from 45 to 12, and at least two Györgys is now the working view (H-076, 75). Third, some of the owner's dates do not fit the pages. The strip filed as 1905 is on the hand-ruled page the register used in the 1830s and 1840s (H-078, 70). The one filed as 1888 gives house 121, the family's house in the 1870s (H-077, 60). A strip filed as 'Maria Demko 1883' reads Zsuzsánna, and one filed as 1783 is of the cholera summer of 1873. The owner has been asked for the page headers. Curiosities: 4

title: The owner's answers: the 2022 land extract shown without names; two jobs left for the end
blurb: No new files. The owner answered three questions from the last report. On the land register extract of 2022: the two owners are probably living, he does not know how they connect to the line, and he kept the file only to show that the name Duška still holds land at Senné. He does not want it held back, only stripped of anything that identifies them. So the document is now public as a de-identified copy, set in type from the text of the original, with the given names, the address, the dates of birth and every register number blacked out; the original file stays out of the repository. The entry for the household no longer gives the two years of birth, and the sheet number is withheld too, since with the village name it leads to the owners in one step in the public register. The earlier batch printed that number and the two years, and the stamped history is not rewritten. On the other two questions, the page headers for five burial strips and the reading of every household of Senné in the census of 1930, his answer is no for now: both come at the end. Curiosities: 0

title: Forty-six burials from Iňačovce: the earliest Duskas of Senné, and a candidate bride who died in the cradle
blurb: The third sub-folder of deaths, sent in four parts and marked final: forty-six strips from the burial register of the Greek Catholic parish of Solymos (Iňačovce), 1812 to 1897. This is the first register in the archive that names itself on the page: the printed sheets of the 1860s are signed by the 'parish priest of Solymos'. Two findings bear on the line. First, the wife of György Duska the elder, Anna Krak, had two candidate baptisms. The likelier one, the Anna born at Jesztreb in October [1848], is now ruled out: she was buried on 8 December, about eight weeks old (H-056 refuted). Three girls called Anna Krak with a father János died at Jesztreb as children, in [1836], [1847] and [1848]. The Sztára baptism rises only from 20 to 25, because nothing new speaks for it. Second, Duskas were at Senné a generation before the Roman Catholic register begins, and they were Greek Catholic: Joannes Duska, a cottar, died there in May 1830 aged 61; a Maria, wife of a Joannes Duska, in December 1829; a widow Anna Duska in the cholera of August [1831]; and Maria Dusko, widow of Georgius, in May 1874 aged 65. That last woman is of an age to be György the elder's mother (H-080, 30), and it is now a little more likely than not that the Roman Catholic Duskas of Senné come from these Greek Catholic ones (H-079, 55). Nobody is added to the tree. Three strips the owner files as Duska are not: one reads Dankó, one Demko, and one is the child of a Dusko mother on the Hrabó farm. Fifteen Demko and Kocsis strips go to the Demko agent. Curiosities: 5

title: Ledger v25: field notes; the burial books get their volume numbers
blurb: No new files. Read ledger v25. It asks each agent for one thing: a page of field notes in the first person, with what it got right and wrong by its own records, its five best curiosities, a report card on every agent including itself, and an account of what it is like to work for the owner. It is in the repository as field-notes/001.md and will not be revised. The agent gives itself a B: the main question is answered on a record, and eighteen of its 81 hypotheses are refuted. The ledger also says the scoring has begun and that its results stay closed to the agents doing the rebuilding; none of it has been opened. Two things came in from the other agents. The Demko agent has read 41 of this repository's burial strips from the images: the two agree on thirty outright and on every file-name date that was set aside, and differ on five readings, which are now written side by side. One of them, whether the Ilona buried in [1836] was a wife of 33 or a child of 3, lowers the case for two men named György Demko from 75 to 65. The Places agent has matched the forms of the Iňačovce burial strips to the archive's four volumes, nos. 380 to 383 at Prešov, so each of the 46 strips of the last batch now carries its volume. Curiosities: 0

title: Twenty-five burials from the Reformed book of Solymos: the other Duskas, with their wives and their ages
blurb: Twenty-five strips from the Reformed burial book of Solymos (Iňačovce), 1830 to 1926; the owner's 'Reform Catholic' is the Calvinist church. Twenty-two are Duska or Dusko, two Kocsis, one Szalontai. None of these people is shown to be kin to the Roman Catholic line of Senné; they are the other Duskas, four kilometres away. What moved. Borbála Plyuchta, first wife of András Duska, was buried in January 1847 aged 43, and András himself in June [1873] aged 78: with a son of his dying in 1854 'both parents alive', the man with two wives (H-063) goes from 60 to 75. Mihály Duska's infant died in 1875 in the house where old János Duska died in 1877, so Mihály is very likely János's son (H-042, 65 to 70). Pál Duska died on 7 June 1838, not in May as first read. György, son of János Duska and Anna Hura, died in 1926 aged 70, in an entry in Slovak that names both parents. Reused names, checked as the ledger asks: Susanna ([1829], died 1830; again [1837]), György ([1870], died of cholera 1873; again 1876), János ([1852], died of cholera 1855). Two hypotheses raised: that Anna Szalontai (died 1834 aged 67) was Pál Duska's wife, held at 30 because it rests on the owner's filing alone; and that János Duska who died in 1883 aged 44 was husband first of Anna Kitko and then of Anna Fedor (45). One strip, 1918, is filed as György Duska; the surname on it does not read Duska to this agent and is recorded unread. The two Kocsis strips go to the Demko agent. Volume reference from the Places agent: Prešov, Lúčky Reformed, Iňačovce filial, no. 592/1. Curiosities: 3

title: Three entries from a Montréal cemetery index: where the great-grandparents lie, and which cemetery holds 'Mikalis'
blurb: Three screenshots from a genealogical society's index to Montréal cemeteries, the whole of the sub-folder 'Montreal'. They are published as crops: the pages show the owner's account on the society's site, and those lines are cut. They close a question open since B-026. The cemetery record of 'Mikalis' Duska (section FT, plot 01965, received 28 November 1965) named no cemetery; the index does: Notre-Dame-des-Neiges (H-068 solved). The same index has the great-grandparents there together: Mary Demko received on 11 September 1950, two days after she died, and Mike Duska on 4 February 1974, the day of the funeral in his death notice, both in section TR, concession 6650. The index is not a death record. It gives the day the cemetery took the body and nothing about age or parents. A small letter matters: a 'd' follows the spouse's name when the spouse was already dead, so Mikalis's wife, Anna Hancosek, died before him. One hypothesis raised (H-084, 40): the census of 1930 gives Mikuláš Duška of Senné a wife Mária, born Hankoščáková, and the cemetery gives Mikalis a wife Anna Hancosek. One surname, two given names: a clerk's slip, or a second wife. That Mikalis is Miklós of Senné, born 28 November 1890, goes from 70 to 75. Curiosities: 1
